notes.claim: Russia undertook obligations to guarantee Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum
notes.context: In December 1994, Ukraine agreed to relinquish the nuclear arsenal it had inherited from the Soviet Union (then the world's third largest) and join the NPT. In return, Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum pledging to respect Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Ukraine and the West regard Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea and 2022 invasion as serious violations of this memorandum. Russia argues that the 2014 Maidan Revolution changed the legal entity of Ukraine, meaning its obligations do not apply to the current government.
notes.verdict: Official record exists (disagreement over legal effect and applicability)

sources.title: Memorandum on Security Assurances in Connection with Ukraine's Accession to the NPT (Budapest Memorandum)

notes.claim: A referendum was held in Crimea in March 2014 and an annexation to Russia was declared
notes.context: On March 16, 2014, a referendum was held in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, then under de facto Russian military control, with official results showing 96.77% in favor of joining Russia. Russia considers this a legitimate exercise of the right to self-determination. On March 27, 2014, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 68/262 (with 100 countries in favor), reaffirming Ukraine's territorial integrity and declaring the referendum invalid. Most countries other than Russia still do not recognize Russian sovereignty over Crimea.
notes.verdict: Referendum held (rejected as invalid by the majority of the international community)

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 68/262: Territorial integrity of Ukraine

notes.claim: The 2014-2015 Minsk Agreements established a ceasefire framework for Donbas, but both sides accused each other of non-compliance
notes.context: Minsk I (September 2014) and Minsk II (February 2015) were ceasefire frameworks agreed upon by Ukraine, Russia, the OSCE, and representatives of the Donetsk/Luhansk People's Republics. Russia claims Ukraine refused the political provisions (granting special status to Donbas; constitutional reforms), while Ukraine argues Russia failed to initiate disarmament and border handover first. Complicating interpretation, French President Macron and former German Chancellor Merkel later suggested the agreements were designed to give Ukraine time to rebuild its military, highlighting the profound gap in how each side understood the accords.
notes.verdict: Agreements exist (disagreement over responsibility for non-compliance)

sources.title: Package of Measures for the Implementation of the Minsk Agreements

notes.claim: It is claimed that at the end of the Cold War, Western nations promised the Soviet Union that NATO would 'not expand one inch eastward'
notes.context: Diplomatic documents record statements made by U.S. Secretary of State James Baker to Soviet President Gorbachev during German reunification negotiations in 1990. Russia cites these as a broken promise and uses them as one basis for justifying the invasion. The U.S. and NATO counter that the remarks were limited to the German context and that no treaty or formal agreement restricting expansion to Central and Eastern Europe was ever concluded. The Helsinki Final Act (1975) enshrines every sovereign state's right to freely choose its alliances, a principle widely held to apply to Ukraine's NATO aspirations.
notes.verdict: Record of statements exists (disagreement over legal bindingness and scope)

notes.claim: Killings of civilians by Russian forces have been confirmed in Bucha and multiple other locations
notes.context: After Russian forces withdrew from areas north of Kyiv in late March 2022, large numbers of civilian bodies were discovered on streets and in buildings in Bucha. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission (OHCHR), the International Criminal Court (ICC), and multiple independent investigators documented evidence of extrajudicial killings, torture, and sexual violence against civilians. In March 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for President Putin in connection with the unlawful deportation of children from Ukraine. Russia claims the Bucha footage was staged and does not recognize the ICC's jurisdiction.
notes.verdict: Documented by the UN and ICC (Russia denies and does not recognize ICC jurisdiction)

sources.title: Ukraine: Situation Report (OHCHR)
sources.publisher: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

sources.title: ICC Arrest Warrant for Vladimir Putin

notes.claim: In September 2022, Russia declared the 'annexation' of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts
notes.context: Referendums were held in Russian-controlled areas from September 23-27, 2022, and on September 30 President Putin declared the annexation of all four oblasts. Official results claimed 87-99% approval, but no international monitors such as the OSCE were present. On October 12, 2022, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution ES-11/4 (143 countries in favor), declaring these 'illegal referendums' void and calling on Russia to withdraw. Russia has enshrined these four oblasts in its constitution as 'indivisible territory.'
notes.verdict: Annexation declaration is a fact (rejected as invalid by the majority of the international community)

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution ES-11/4

notes.claim: On February 25, 2022, Russia vetoed a UN Security Council draft resolution condemning the invasion of Ukraine.
notes.context: On February 25, 2022, the UN Security Council voted on a draft resolution demanding Russia's immediate withdrawal, but Russia exercised its veto to block it (11 in favor, 1 against, 3 abstentions: China, India, UAE). This triggered the convening of the 11th Emergency Special Session under the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution, which adopted Resolution ES-11/1 with overwhelming support (141 in favor, 5 against, 35 abstentions), though without binding force. The structural problem of the Security Council — that permanent members can veto resolutions concerning their own actions — once again sparked international debate.
notes.verdict: The veto is a matter of record (ES-11/1 adoption also confirmed)

sources.title: UN General Assembly Emergency Special Session Resolution ES-11/1

notes.claim: In March 2022, the ICJ issued provisional measures ordering Russia to immediately suspend military operations in Ukraine.
notes.context: On February 27, 2022, Ukraine filed a case against Russia at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on grounds of violations of the Genocide Convention. On March 16, 2022, the ICJ issued provisional measures ordering Russia to 'immediately suspend the military operations that it commenced on 24 February 2022' (13 in favor, 2 against). Russia denied the ICJ's jurisdiction and ignored the order, continuing military operations. This case is widely cited as a landmark example of the limits of international legal enforcement mechanisms.
notes.verdict: Provisional measures order is a matter of record (Russia refused to comply and denied jurisdiction)

sources.title: Allegations of Genocide under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Ukraine v. Russian Federation) — ICJ

notes.claim: From autumn 2024, North Korea was reported to have deployed troops to support Russia's military operations
notes.context: In October 2024, the governments of the United States, South Korea, and Ukraine announced that North Korea had deployed approximately 10,000 ground troops to Russia. Multiple UN Security Council member states presented corroborating evidence — including satellite imagery and intercepted communications. While both North Korea and Russia initially denied the deployment, by late 2024 President Putin had made statements that effectively acknowledged a degree of North Korean military participation. The UN Panel of Experts had already documented North Korean supplies of artillery shells and missiles to Russia as early as 2023. Ukraine stated it had taken North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war and expressed its intent to seek access to them.
notes.verdict: Deployment confirmed by multiple governments and international bodies (Russia and DPRK initially denied, later partially acknowledged)

sources.title: UN Panel of Experts Report on DPRK sanctions — military cooperation with Russia

notes.claim: In 2024, F-16 fighter jets were transferred to Ukraine under an initiative led by Denmark and the Netherlands
notes.context: In August 2024, NATO-operated F-16 fighter jets were delivered to Ukraine — led by Denmark and the Netherlands — and the Ukrainian Air Force began operational deployment. This marked the first transfer of advanced jet fighters that Ukraine had been seeking since the start of the war. The United States authorized the transfer, but imposed conditions prohibiting the use of these aircraft for strikes on Russian territory. Russia condemned the transfer as a form of direct NATO intervention in the conflict and claimed it significantly raised the risk of escalation.
notes.verdict: Transfer is a matter of record (Russia criticizes it as NATO intervention; usage restriction conditions applied)

sources.title: Ukraine receives first F-16 fighter jets from Denmark and the Netherlands

notes.claim: The IAEA has repeatedly issued safety warnings regarding the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, which is under Russian occupation
notes.context: Ukraine's largest nuclear power plant, the Zaporizhzhia NPP (6,000 MW; Europe's largest), was seized by Russian forces in March 2022. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) deployed a permanent monitoring mission to the facility and has repeatedly expressed concern about shelling near the plant, repeated severing of external power supplies, and reliance on emergency diesel generators. With each side blaming the other for the attacks, attribution has proven extremely difficult. IAEA Director General Grossi warned that 'each time one of the seven pillars of nuclear safety is violated, we are a step closer to a nuclear accident.' The plant remains under Russian military control, and its connection to Ukraine's power grid has remained unstable.
notes.verdict: IAEA monitoring and warnings are a matter of record (both sides blame each other for shelling)

sources.title: IAEA Reports on Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant

notes.claim: In August 2024, the Ukrainian military launched a large-scale cross-border operation into Russia's Kursk Oblast
notes.context: On August 6, 2024, Ukrainian forces crossed into Russia's Kursk Oblast, temporarily seizing several hundred square kilometers of Russian territory. This was the largest-scale Ukrainian incursion into Russian territory since the invasion began on February 24, 2022. The Ukrainian government explained the operation as designed to 'raise pressure on Russia in negotiations and to stretch the front line.' The Russian government designated it a 'terrorist act' and began evacuating residents of Kursk. Facing a major Russian counteroffensive by late 2024, Ukraine lost most of the territory it had seized, but the operation's political and psychological impact was significant.
notes.verdict: The operation and cross-border seizure of territory are confirmed facts (assessments of its strategic rationale and long-term effects remain debated)

notes.claim: The Black Sea Grain Initiative, concluded in July 2022, collapsed in July 2023 when Russia announced its withdrawal
notes.context: Russia's invasion of Ukraine blocked grain and food exports from Ukraine, raising the risk of a global food crisis. In July 2022, the UN and Turkey brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which allowed the resumption of grain exports from Ukraine's major ports, including Odesa. In July 2023, Russia announced its withdrawal from the deal, stating that restrictions on Russian agricultural and fertilizer exports had not been lifted, and the agreement effectively collapsed. During the period the initiative was in force, approximately 33 million metric tons of foodstuffs were exported. The collapse had severe consequences for food-importing countries in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
notes.verdict: Both the signing and the collapse are matters of record (disagreement over the scale of impact and attribution of responsibility)

sources.title: Black Sea Grain Initiative — United Nations

notes.claim: Iran has been reported to have supplied Russia with large quantities of Shahed-series kamikaze drones
notes.context: Western governments, Ukraine, and the UN Panel of Experts have reported that from the second half of 2022, Iran supplied Russia with large numbers of 'Shahed-136' series one-way attack drones, which Russian forces have widely used in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure and urban areas. Iran initially denied the transfers, but from 2023 onward, statements appeared acknowledging that some supplies had occurred prior to the invasion. The United States and the European Union imposed additional sanctions on Iran over the transfers. While Ukraine's air defenses have shot down many of these drones, the sustained drone assaults strain Ukraine's air-defense resources in an attritional campaign.
notes.verdict: Transfers confirmed by multiple governments and international bodies (Iran initially denied, later partially acknowledged)
